title: Roseanne's Return

jokes.text: Staff is watching O.J. trial coverage on TV during what is supposed to be a staff meeting, and Larry has to call the meeting to order
jokes.setup: A production meeting is called ostensibly to address the show's creative malaise
jokes.punchline: Everyone is transfixed by OJ trial coverage, watching it instead of engaging with the meeting — the meeting about freshness is itself stale
jokes.explanation: A solid scene-setting gag. The irony of a meeting about keeping the show fresh being derailed by the most culturally dominant distraction of 1995 lands cleanly, with no dialogue needed. Good economy, modest originality.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: hey now... oh, started on time

jokes.text: Hank arrives late to the meeting and announces proudly: 'Hey now... oh, started on time.'
jokes.setup: Larry calls a meeting to address the show's malaise; staff gathers
jokes.punchline: Hank waltzes in late and expresses mild surprise/credit that it started without him, as if his absence caused the punctuality
jokes.explanation: A perfectly Hank moment — self-important, oblivious, delivered with the signature 'Hey now.' Four words that reveal his entire worldview. High character integration because this is exclusively a Hank joke. Economy is exceptional.

dialogue.line: Kato kaelin has people?

jokes.text: Larry asks for ideas to keep the show fresh. Someone says 'Better guests?' Someone else says 'Better jokes.' Then: 'I'm sorry, were we supposed to come with ideas?'
jokes.setup: Larry solicits creative input from his staff at a meeting explicitly called to generate ideas
jokes.punchline: A staff member sincerely asks if they were supposed to come prepared with ideas — perfectly capturing the passive, reactive Hollywood TV culture
jokes.explanation: Sharp, quick, industry-specific observational comedy. The gag is that this is a writer's room without writers — everyone is sycophant or bureaucrat. Clean structure, good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Hank's property values complaint about living on Rockingham

jokes.text: Kato Kaelin's booker suggests him as a guest; the room dismisses it, but then: 'Kato Kaelin has people?'
jokes.setup: Paula mentions that Kato Kaelin's 'people' keep calling about a booking
jokes.punchline: Larry's incredulous 'Kato Kaelin has people?' punctures the absurdity of OJ-trial celebrity — the pool boy with a publicist
jokes.explanation: Four words, perfectly placed. The joke exploits the absurdity of OJ-trial micro-celebrity with laser precision — Kato Kaelin as accidental star has people? The economy is outstanding. Earns its score through specificity and timing.

dialogue.line: you bumped him for faith ford.
Hey, who knew he was going to get this hot?

jokes.text: Staff member laments the real victims of the OJ crime: his property values on Rockingham, the tourist barricade, the detour past canyon view, the left turn on Sunset with 'no fucking light'
jokes.setup: Conversation about OJ's cultural impact shifts to a moment of apparent sincerity — 'the real victims of this crime'
jokes.punchline: The 'real victim' is revealed to be the speaker's property value and commute time, with escalating petty grievances, culminating in traffic-light rage
jokes.explanation: Genuinely funny bit of LA industry-bubble satire. The escalation from solemn ('real victims') to the profane pettiness of traffic routing is structurally sharp. The 'no fucking light' as the terminal complaint is a great button. Strong earned comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: This is just what we needed. A sense of direction. Here we go. Hank.

jokes.text: 'Is that the same suit O.J. wore the last time we did the show?' / 'No, last time he was on, you bumped him for Faith Ford. Hey, who knew he was going to get this hot?'
jokes.setup: OJ is referenced; someone notes a suit
jokes.punchline: The revelation that OJ was bumped for Faith Ford — and regret that a murder suspect's notoriety wasn't anticipated — treats OJ's infamy as a mere booking opportunity missed
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's sharpest satirical thrust at the intersection of TV booking culture and OJ spectacle. 'Who knew he was going to get this hot?' applied to a double-murder suspect is darkly brilliant — perfectly capturing the moral vacuum of late-night TV production. High originality and earned comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Well, aren't you a goddamn smart fellow because it was at planet fucking Hollywood. I mean who wants to eat buffalo wings sitting next to demi Moore's torn panties from disclosure?

jokes.text: Roseanne is announced as a Wednesday guest. Larry says: 'Roseanne?' Then immediately: 'Well, all right. The meeting's over!'
jokes.setup: Meeting is ostensibly about direction and fresh content; Larry is facilitating
jokes.punchline: The mere mention of Roseanne's name causes Larry to snap-end the meeting and declare it a success — his panic disguised as enthusiasm, immediately transparent
jokes.explanation: Larry's flight instinct masquerading as executive decisiveness is perfectly in character. The abruptness is the joke. High character integration — this is Larry's defining anxiety-driven comedic mode.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Oh, stop. I smell sulfur.

jokes.text: Larry didn't go to Roseanne's wedding because it was at Planet Hollywood: 'Who wants to eat buffalo wings sitting next to Demi Moore's torn panties from Disclosure?'
jokes.setup: Artie thought Larry went to Roseanne's wedding; Larry insists he didn't
jokes.punchline: The rationale for skipping: the venue (Planet Hollywood) and specifically having to eat near Demi Moore's movie-prop underwear on display
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The specificity — 'Demi Moore's torn panties from Disclosure' — is what elevates this from a generic Hollywood-tackiness joke to something genuinely inspired. The image is vivid and absurd, and Larry's fastidiousness about where he eats is perfect character work. High quotability and originality.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: She puts the supe in super model.

jokes.text: Larry describes seeing Roseanne in the front seat of the limo making out with the limo driver. Artie: 'All right! How many times do we have to go through this story?'
jokes.setup: Larry is building up to a story about his humiliation
jokes.punchline: Artie's weary 'How many times do we have to go through this story?' signals this is Larry's obsessive grievance — it's a known routine, which is funnier than the story itself
jokes.explanation: Artie's interruption does more comedic work than the story — it confirms Larry's neurotic obsessiveness without needing exposition. Good economy, strong character integration for both Larry and Artie.

dialogue.speaker: Ivanka
dialogue.line: because when they kill tuna, they kill dolphins, and dolphins are people. People of the sea.

jokes.text: That's great. It'll be fireworks. / Oh, stop. I smell sulfur.
jokes.setup: Artie says an on-air reunion with Roseanne will be 'fireworks'
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'I smell sulfur' — taking Artie's metaphor and running it to its dark, literal conclusion, expressing genuine dread through wordplay
jokes.explanation: Larry's extension of the fireworks metaphor to sulfur is a clever wordplay move that also functions as character comedy — his anxiety expressed through a witty deflection. Economical and sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: They're fish, they're not people. Fish. The fight ends in fish.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Ivanka's on Thursday. She's slim and sexy. She puts the supe in supermodel.'
jokes.setup: Artie is trying to distract Larry from his Roseanne anxiety with a booking pivot
jokes.punchline: 'She puts the supe in supermodel' — a half-nonsense portmanteau compliment delivered with Artie's gruff sincerity
jokes.explanation: Mild wordplay that works primarily as a Rip Torn character moment — Artie's blunt, old-school charisma makes it charming if not exactly sharp. The pun is functional but not inspired.

dialogue.speaker: Ivanka
dialogue.line: The lingerie catalog really fucked me...

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: The lingerie catalog fucked you?

jokes.text: Larry orders tuna. Ivanka: 'Except for tuna, because when they kill tuna, they kill dolphins, and dolphins are people. People of the sea.'
jokes.setup: Larry tries to order tuna to match Ivanka
jokes.punchline: Ivanka's objection is that dolphins are 'people — people of the sea,' delivered with total sincerity as though this is a considered philosophical position
jokes.explanation: 'People of the sea' is a genuinely funny, quotable absurdist phrase — it works because it's delivered as sincere advocacy, capturing the beautiful-person-who-has-never-had-a-hard-thought archetype. Good economy and structure.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Oh, fuck.

jokes.text: Larry tries swordfish instead. Ivanka approves: 'They're fish. They're fish, they're not people. Fish. The fight ends in fish.'
jokes.setup: Ivanka has banned tuna due to dolphin solidarity
jokes.punchline: 'The fight ends in fish' — delivered as a solemn verdict, as if swordfish's non-person status has been carefully adjudicated
jokes.explanation: 'The fight ends in fish' is a beautifully strange punchline — the rhythm and finality of it is what makes it quotable. It escalates the absurdist dolphin-logic into a pseudo-legal ruling. One of the episode's best individual lines.

dialogue.speaker: Ivanka
dialogue.line: Do svidaniya.

jokes.text: Ivanka mentions the lingerie catalog 'really fucked me' again. Larry: 'Pardon me?' Ivanka repeats it. Larry: 'The lingerie catalog fucked you?' Then: 'If I had to do what you do... I don't know how you do it.'
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to maintain a date-like conversation; Ivanka is processing her professional grievances
jokes.punchline: Larry's sympathetic 'I don't know how you do it' applied to the harrowing ordeal of being a lingerie model reveals his helpless sycophancy with beautiful women
jokes.explanation: Larry's toadying capitulation to beauty is a good character beat. The joke works through cringe — his sincerity about how hard modeling must be. Moderate impact.

dialogue.speaker: Roseanne
dialogue.line: Larry, you asshole, I know you're there. It's roseanne. Call me if you have the balls.

jokes.text: Ivanka describes her TV pilot: 'I play a maiden. Jeff Conaway plays the divorced dad.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks about her pilot to keep the date-conversation going
jokes.punchline: A medieval-themed pilot starring Jeff Conaway — the combination of casting and character description is inherently absurd as a Hollywood artifact
jokes.explanation: Jeff Conaway as the divorced dad in a period maiden drama is funny by pure absurdity of casting, but the joke doesn't fully land — it needs a reaction beat that isn't quite there. Competent.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Did letterman have Tom hanks on again, or... Did Leno have the ito dancers on again?

jokes.text: After the date, Ivanka says 'I really like you. Do you want to see me again?' — and continues repeating this across an awkward silence/phone moment. Larry is clearly distracted.
jokes.setup: Date seems to have gone well; Ivanka is expressing genuine interest
jokes.punchline: Larry's distraction (checking phone, OJ coverage in background) is obvious; the earnest repetition of 'Do you want to see me again?' becomes increasingly sad and comic
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is structural — Larry's total inability to be present with an attractive, interested woman because of his neurotic obsession with Roseanne and the show. Works as cringe, less as joke.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Harrison ford, Steve Martin, Michelle pfeiffer. Who else?

jokes.text: Roseanne's voicemail to Larry: 'Larry, you asshole, I know you're there... Call me if you have the balls.'
jokes.setup: We hear the OJ trial on TV — Larry is screening his calls
jokes.punchline: Roseanne's machine message cuts through with her characteristic bluntness — 'call me if you have the balls' perfectly captures the power dynamic reversal
jokes.explanation: The message is funny because it's exactly what you'd expect from Roseanne (both the character and the real person). High character integration — both for the fictional Roseanne and for Larry's complete deflation when he hears it. The contrast with the OJ coverage playing underneath is a nice comic juxtaposition.

dialogue.speaker: Fan
dialogue.line: Are you Larry Sanders?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: Larry calls Beverly at 2am to ask about a therapist. Beverly: 'Did letterman have Tom Hanks on again?' / 'Did Leno have the Ito dancers on again?'
jokes.setup: Larry calls his assistant at 2am, clearly distressed; Beverly tries to identify the cause of his anxiety
jokes.punchline: Beverly's two diagnostic questions — Letterman/Tom Hanks and Leno/Ito dancers — reveal that Larry's known pathologies are watching competitors' bookings at night. The Ito dancers are a real, absurd 1995 late-night moment.
jokes.explanation: Beverly's two questions serve as a perfect comedic taxonomy of Larry's anxieties — he's not anxious about life, he's anxious about the talk show war. 'Did Leno have the Ito dancers on again?' is a brilliantly specific 1995 industry detail. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What brings you here?

dialogue.speaker: Chevy
dialogue.line: The show get cancelled?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: No, no. No, not yet.

jokes.text: Larry asks who Dr. Reisman sees. Beverly: 'Harrison Ford, Steve Martin, Michelle Pfeiffer.' Long pause. Larry: 'Who else?'
jokes.setup: Larry asks about the psychiatrist's celebrity clientele as a quality signal
jokes.punchline: The long pause after three A-listers followed by 'Who else?' — Larry needs a longer list before committing, or is disappointed these aren't his tier
jokes.explanation: Two words — 'Who else?' — after a 14-second pause do enormous comedic work. The joke is Larry's simultaneous insecurity (is he A-list enough for this shrink?) and vanity (three stars aren't enough to impress him). Exceptional economy and character integration.

dialogue.line: I thought it was 19 months.
On the 12th.
Right.

jokes.text: In the waiting room, a stranger asks 'Excuse me, are you Larry Sanders?' Larry: 'No.'
jokes.setup: Larry is in a psychiatrist's waiting room, presumably trying to maintain privacy
jokes.punchline: Larry flatly denies his own identity — immediate, no hesitation, full denial — to a person he will presumably see again in the building
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — one word, Larry's entire psychology. The psychiatry setting makes it funnier: the man who can't face himself won't even admit his name. Perfect character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Chevy
dialogue.line: I had a fish behind my head... everybody said, 'fish? Why fish?' I don't know. Why fish?

jokes.text: Chevy Chase is also in the waiting room. They greet warmly. 'What brings you here? The show get cancelled?' / 'No. No. Not yet. That's not why I'm here either.'
jokes.setup: Larry runs into a familiar face at the shrink — immediately assumes the worst
jokes.punchline: 'No, not yet.' — Chevy's qualification is the joke: he doesn't deny the show might get cancelled, just that it's not the reason today. Self-deprecating from a famously troubled TV career.
jokes.explanation: Chevy Chase playing a version of himself at a psychiatrist's office, with 'Not yet' referring to his show's cancellation, is sharp celebrity self-awareness. It works on two levels — character comedy and meta-comedy about Chevy's actual career. High earned comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Hello, mayor. Hank Kingsley. Listen, a little problem. Easy fix.

jokes.text: Chevy: 'I should never have done that show. Well... I had a fish behind my head. Everybody said, fish? Why fish? I don't know. Why fish?'
jokes.setup: Chevy explains why he's in therapy post-Chevy Chase Show failure
jokes.punchline: The fish — an actual infamous failed set design decision from his show — becomes the symbol of his creative collapse, and his inability to explain it is the joke
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout jokes. The Chevy Chase Show's actual set had a fish motif that was widely mocked — Chevy's baffled, recursive self-questioning ('Why fish? I don't know. Why fish?') is both a real showbiz confession and meta-comedy about celebrity self-destruction. Exceptionally high character integration and earned comedy — works only because Chevy Chase is playing himself interrogating his real failure.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: You could say that, uh, you live on rockingham, just a knife's throw from o.j.'s house.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Uh, no. I don't think I could do that one. That... that... that implies o.j. Is guilty.

jokes.text: No, not yet. / That's not why I'm here either. / Oh.
jokes.setup: Larry asks if Chevy's show got cancelled (implying that would be the obvious reason for therapy)
jokes.punchline: Chevy's 'No, not yet' — acknowledging the cancellation is coming — followed by his 'that's not why I'm here either' — mutually acknowledging they're both in therapy without admitting why
jokes.explanation: 'No, not yet' is the perfect self-aware response — Chevy acknowledging the inevitable with studied nonchalance. The mutual 'that's not why I'm here either' creates a comedy of shared denial between two men clearly in crisis. Economy is strong.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm sure if you looked at all my underwear you'd find some blood there, too.

jokes.text: Larry asks: 'So let me get this straight. You proposed to Roseanne when you were taking the pills?' / 'No, she helped me get off the pills and then I proposed to her.' / 'So you were off the pills when you proposed? Interesting.'
jokes.setup: Therapist session; they discuss the Roseanne relationship history
jokes.punchline: 'Interesting' — the therapist's non-committal, loaded professional response. The joke is Larry trying to construct a narrative where his behavior was chemically induced, only to have the therapist close off that exit
jokes.explanation: Efficient therapy-scene joke — Larry's self-serving framing meets the therapist's impeccably neutral 'Interesting,' which lands as deadpan punctuation. Well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, I'm... I'm going to go out and murder someone without my shoes on. Come on, come on.

jokes.text: Dr. Reisman tells Larry: 'If you don't want her on the show, you don't have her on the show. It's your life.' Larry: 'Artie wouldn't understand that.' / 'Forget Artie. He's a producer. It's his job to put the show first.'
jokes.setup: The therapist is giving empowering advice
jokes.punchline: The therapist's dismissal of Artie as 'just a producer' — pragmatically accurate but spoken with the detachment of someone who doesn't know Artie — sets up the upcoming collision perfectly
jokes.explanation: Functional setup beat — the irony of a therapist telling you to ignore the most competent person in your professional life is mildly funny, and it plants a seed for Artie's later response. Modest impact.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: He's always been nice to me.

jokes.text: Hank calls the mayor's office to complain about the OJ tourist barricade on Rockingham: 'I'm a celebrity. I like gawkers. What I don't like is having to drive 8 full minutes out of my way followed by gawkers.'
jokes.setup: Hank is making an official complaint about infrastructure problems caused by OJ tourism
jokes.punchline: The distinction is purely Hank: he LIKES gawkers as a general principle (celebrity validation), he just objects to the inconvenient routing. Eight full minutes of his time.
jokes.explanation: This is pure Hank Kingsley — the layered absurdity that he doesn't want LESS celebrity attention, just better-routed celebrity attention. 'I'm a celebrity. I like gawkers.' is an extraordinary sentence. High character integration — only Hank would frame this as a civic rights issue.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: if o.j. Had really just admitted he was guilty from the get-go, he'd be out by now.

jokes.text: Hank asks Phil the warm-up comedian to give him a new joke because his Clinton inhaling bit 'just isn't getting that WHAAAA laugh it used to.'
jokes.setup: Hank approaches Phil about refreshing his material
jokes.punchline: The sound effect Hank makes — 'WHAAAA' — to describe the desired audience reaction is funnier than any joke he could tell, and his earnestness about it reveals his insecurity
jokes.explanation: Hank's onomatopoeia for the desired big laugh is a perfect detail — it's both sad (he knows the laugh has faded) and funny (his attempt to articulate it). Strong character work.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: The latest DNA study now shows o.j. Didn't even gain those 2,000 yards that year.

jokes.text: Phil suggests a joke: 'You live on Rockingham, just a knife's throw from O.J.'s house.' Hank: 'That implies O.J. is guilty. I don't think he is.'
jokes.setup: Phil offers a topical Rockingham/OJ joke for Hank to use
jokes.punchline: Hank refuses on grounds that it implies guilt — revealing his sincere OJ defense position, which is funnier and darker than any joke Phil could have written
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Hank's sincere OJ innocence belief is funnier than any OJ joke. The phrase 'knife's throw' from Phil is perfectly constructed — deliberately evocative — and Hank's objection is deadpan perfect. Strong structure, very high character integration.

dialogue.line: women married to American presidents who cheat on them with fat blonde whores

jokes.text: Uh, no. I don't think I could do that one. That... that... that implies O.J. is guilty. Uh-huh. Oh, I... I don't... I don't think he is.
jokes.setup: Phil pitches the 'knife's throw' joke; Larry declines it
jokes.punchline: Larry's earnest 'I don't think he is' — Larry Sanders, host of a late-night show, apparently genuinely believing O.J. is innocent, delivered with the complete sincerity of a man who has rationalized his entertainment industry contacts
jokes.explanation: Larry's O.J. belief functions as a joke about how proximity to celebrity warps judgment — the same Larry who worried about his show booking O.J. is now defending him. The stutter adds comedic texture. Sets up the Hank conversation beautifully.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I flushed them down the toilet with the rest of tonight's show.

jokes.text: Hank, please don't tell me you're one of those. / Hey, I have met this man. He's always been nice to me. He is a great guest. He's a good neighbor, always kept his lawn up.
jokes.setup: Phil expresses disbelief at Hank's O.J. defense
jokes.punchline: 'He's a good neighbor, always kept his lawn up' — Hank's character assessment of a murder suspect bottoming out at lawn maintenance
jokes.explanation: Hank's defense of O.J. descends from 'he's been nice to me' (already absurd) to 'great guest' (showbiz absurd) to 'always kept his lawn up' — the most banal possible character reference. The lawn detail is the perfect landing point. Strong character integration: Hank's world view runs on personal niceties and neighborly propriety.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Well, let's call Dr. Reisman for a last-minute booking idea.

jokes.text: Hank's OJ defense: 'He's always been nice to me. He's a great guest. He's a good neighbor, always kept his lawn up.' Phil: 'What about all the evidence? What about all that blood?' Hank: 'I'm sure if you looked at all my underwear you'd find some blood there, too.'
jokes.setup: Phil challenges Hank's OJ innocence belief with the physical evidence
jokes.punchline: Hank's counterargument — that blood in underwear is universal and proves nothing — is both a gross non-sequitur and a perfect encapsulation of Hank's reasoning being grounded entirely in personal relationship
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest moments. Hank's logic is impenetrable and grotesque — of course everyone has bloody underwear, so the bloody socks prove nothing. It's dark comedy about the stupidity of loyalty-based reasoning, delivered as absolutely sincere debate. High originality, structure, and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Then he can produce the show, and you can come to my office, lie on my couch, and cry about your mammy.

jokes.text: Phil: 'I can't believe I'm having this conversation with you.' Hank: 'What?' — Beat. Phil just stares.
jokes.setup: Phil has tried every logical argument against Hank's OJ defense
jokes.punchline: Phil's exhausted meta-comment and Hank's genuine bafflement create a perfect beat — Hank doesn't understand why this conversation is remarkable
jokes.explanation: Good button to the OJ exchange. Phil's disbelief and Hank's genuine incomprehension is a well-executed reaction beat. The silence after 'What?' is where the laugh lives.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Soon you'll have Larry recovering a false memory of an uncle who tried to touch his pecker.

jokes.text: Hank: 'I am freaking out.' — after the egging conversation, said with theatrical self-pity
jokes.setup: Phil has delivered a devastating logical rebuttal
jokes.punchline: Hank's response to being unable to defend his OJ position is existential crisis — 'I am freaking out' — which is wildly out of proportion
jokes.explanation: Mild Hank moment. His dramatic self-declaration works as character beat but doesn't have a strong punchline mechanism — it's more of a tag.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm sorry. I thought you got a good spot from years of hard work. Turns out all you have to do is dive into a shallow pond.

jokes.text: Larry's monologue: 'I don't want to say it's been going long, but if O.J. had just admitted he was guilty from the get-go, he'd be out by now.'
jokes.setup: Larry addresses the audience about the length of the OJ trial
jokes.punchline: The joke inverts the legal logic — admitting guilt early would have been strategically faster (shorter sentence than trial time) — while casually assuming guilt
jokes.explanation: A solid monologue joke — the timing-based logic (admit guilt, do less time) is clean and dark. Good structure, modest originality. Works better in 1995 context when trial length was the dominant complaint.

dialogue.speaker: Roseanne
dialogue.line: Tell that limp dick asshole if he wants to bump me he should have the balls to do it himself, or I'm going to come down there and beat his fat ass just the way he likes it.

jokes.text: Larry: 'The latest DNA study now shows O.J. didn't even gain those 2,000 yards that year.'
jokes.setup: Following an OJ guilt joke, pivoting to 'DNA study'
jokes.punchline: The DNA study reveals nothing forensic — it reveals he underperformed in his 1973 NFL season. Misdirection from trial DNA to sports statistics.
jokes.explanation: Sharp misdirection — 'DNA study' sets up forensics, delivers sports revisionism. The non-sequitur pivot is well-timed and the internal logic (DNA debunks the 2,000-yard season) is pleasingly absurd. Good economy.

dialogue.line: I just said that I liked it.

jokes.text: Larry to a standing audience member mid-monologue: 'See? You're sorry you stood, aren't you?'
jokes.setup: An audience member apparently stood up for something (applause or leaving)
jokes.punchline: Larry turns it into a meta-moment — the audience member's standing is reframed as regret about Larry's monologue quality
jokes.explanation: A quick self-deprecating aside that works because of its brevity. Larry's ability to weaponize the audience's actions against himself/them is a nice talk-show-host comedy mode.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Perhaps you could arrange a conference call between you, Dr. Reisman, and the 12 roseannes.

jokes.text: Chevy arrives backstage: 'When I saw Larry at the shrink today, he said drop by.' Artie: 'When was that?' Artie then processes it: 'Oh, right. At the shrink.'
jokes.setup: Chevy mentions casually that he saw Larry at the psychiatrist's office
jokes.punchline: Artie's double-take — 'When was that?' then the deflated 'Oh, right. At the shrink.' — reveals this is new information he's absorbing with barely-concealed disapproval
jokes.explanation: Rip Torn's reaction is where the comedy lives — Artie's barely-contained 'Oh, right. At the shrink.' is a masterclass in loaded understatement. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You little prick!

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You did it! You egged my car!

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: What are you talking about?

jokes.text: Larry's monologue: Hillary Clinton on Oprah — 'Yes, the title of the show was: Women Married to American Presidents Who Cheat on Them with Fat Blonde Whores.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks if anyone saw Hillary Clinton on Oprah
jokes.punchline: The episode title — a full, vulgar Oprah-style title that names exactly what it is, spoken as if announcing a real broadcast
jokes.explanation: Effective in its bluntness — the Oprah-title format applied to a presidential scandal is a good structural choice. The profanity is the button. Decent impact, but the joke slightly overshoots — the specificity of 'fat blonde whores' is more provocative than funny.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: I am 100% not guilty.

jokes.text: Artie confronts Larry backstage: 'I'm doing the monologue and you're talking to Chevy Chase at the monitor, and then Beverly, and then you're muttering to yourself at one point. Where are your pants?'
jokes.setup: Artie is cataloguing Larry's distractions during the live monologue
jokes.punchline: 'Where are your pants?' — the escalation from reasonable professional concerns to the surreal detail that Larry is pantsless mid-monologue
jokes.explanation: The list builds beautifully — talking to Chevy, then Beverly, then muttering — and 'Where are your pants?' lands as a perfect comic climax. The pants reveal is completely unexpected and the deadpan delivery makes it sublime. The escalation structure earns a high score.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: Fuck you, Hank. Of course I did it. Fuck you! Fuck you! Fuck you!

jokes.text: Larry: 'I flushed them down the toilet with the rest of tonight's show.'
jokes.setup: Artie asks where Larry's pants are
jokes.punchline: Larry's pants went the same way as tonight's show — down the toilet — delivered as equal-weight self-assessment of his professional and literal situation
jokes.explanation: A beautiful line. The metaphorical and literal are unified — the show is a disaster and so is Larry's attire. The economy is outstanding: pants and professional dignity share the same fate. One of Shandling's best deliveries imagined.

dialogue.speaker: Roseanne
dialogue.line: I can't wear this dress! I'm pregnant, you dip shit!

jokes.text: Artie: 'Who'd you get to replace Roseanne? Did you get anybody?' Larry: 'Oh, yes indeed. Mr. Richard Simmons.' Artie: 'Oh, good.' Larry: 'That's the best you could do? Richard Simmons?'
jokes.setup: Artie already knew Larry bumped Roseanne; now learning the replacement
jokes.punchline: Artie's cheerful 'Oh, good' at Richard Simmons as replacement is then undercut by Larry immediately questioning his own decision — Larry criticizes himself before Artie can
jokes.explanation: Good Larry-Artie dynamic comedy. Artie's non-ironic 'Oh, good' is perfect — he'll work with Richard Simmons, no problem. Larry's instant self-critique ('That's the best you could do?') before Artie has a chance to criticize is sharp character insight.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: This television show is where you are in total command, where no one gets the best of you, where you are the king.

jokes.text: He does not make any decisions, I make the decisions, OK? / Then he can produce the show, and you can come to my office, lie on my couch, and cry about your mammy.
jokes.setup: Larry insists Dr. Reisman has no production authority
jokes.punchline: Artie's offer — swap roles, Larry cries about his mammy — is a dismissive escalation that reveals Artie's actual contempt for the therapy setup while offering the most reductive description of what he thinks Larry is doing there
jokes.explanation: 'Lie on my couch and cry about your mammy' is a wonderfully specific and contemptuous phrase — 'mammy' in particular is pitch-perfect for Artie's old-school sensibility. The role-swap offer is structured well: Artie will produce, Larry can be the patient. Character integration is excellent — only Artie talks like this.

dialogue.speaker: Roseanne
dialogue.line: Just then, when you didn't know whether to kiss me or not.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Well, let's call Dr. Reisman for a last-minute booking idea.' Larry: 'He does not make any decisions, I make the decisions.' Artie: 'Then he can produce the show, and you can come to my office, lie on my couch, and cry about your mammy.'
jokes.setup: Larry tries to assert his autonomy citing the therapist's advice
jokes.punchline: Artie's counter-offer — Larry can lie on HIS couch and cry about 'your mammy' — is a withering dismissal that reframes therapy as self-indulgence
jokes.explanation: 'Lie on my couch and cry about your mammy' is a line that could only come from Artie — gruff, dismissive of psychological language, absolutely cutting. High character integration for Rip Torn's Artie, who is the voice of pragmatic contempt throughout.

dialogue.speaker: Roseanne
dialogue.line: because it had a penis and a brain.

jokes.text: Artie confronts Dr. Reisman backstage: 'Soon you'll have Larry recovering a false memory of an uncle who tried to touch his pecker.'
jokes.setup: Artie tries to establish ground rules with the psychiatrist about Larry's treatment
jokes.punchline: The 'false memory' / 'touch his pecker' line — Artie's hyperbolic prediction of where therapy leads, delivered with contempt and comic precision
jokes.explanation: Rip Torn's Artie is at his most Artie here — the 'pecker' line is blunt, specific, and perfectly calibrated contempt for the therapy industry. It references a real 1990s cultural panic (repressed memory) and weaponizes it as Artie's darkest prediction. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I guess I would feel competitive over... in the breast feeding area. I think that I would be there, uh, you know, nudging the child out of the way.

jokes.text: Hank arrives at work furious: 'God damn it. Somebody egged my fucking car!'
jokes.setup: Morning at the studio; Hank arrives
jokes.punchline: The fact of the egging itself, and Hank's operatic fury at what is a minor inconvenience — it's the scale of his response to petty vandalism that's funny
jokes.explanation: Good premise-establishing beat. The egging itself is funny as a concept (Hank being egged) but the joke here is mostly setup for the extended sequence that follows.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: It will be 18 years before you see another one. That's what I would say.

jokes.text: Hank discovers his parking space — the closest one — is a handicapped spot given to Bill Hanson, a paraplegic. Hank: 'Oh, I'm sorry. I thought you got a good spot from years of hard work. Turns out all you have to do is dive into a shallow pond.'
jokes.setup: Hank resents not having the prime parking spot, given to Bill Hanson
jokes.punchline: The reveal that Bill Hanson is a paraplegic, followed immediately by Hank's 'all you have to do is dive into a shallow pond' — weaponizing disability into a career strategy complaint
jokes.explanation: This is among the episode's best jokes. The structural setup (years of hard work → paraplegic parking) followed by the devastating 'all you have to do is dive into a shallow pond' is dark comedy of the highest Hank order. It's deeply wrong and completely character-consistent. High originality, structure, and character integration — only Hank would say this, only Hank would mean it sincerely as a grievance. The shallow pond specificity is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Roseanne
dialogue.line: Yeah, but my show's funny.

jokes.text: 'I can't imagine why anyone would want to egg your car.' — said with perfect deadpan after the parking spot grievance
jokes.setup: Hank is genuinely baffled about who egged his car and why
jokes.punchline: The deadpan 'I can't imagine why anyone would want to egg your car' — ironic commentary on Hank's obliviousness about his own behavior
jokes.explanation: Classic deadpan setup. The line lands because Hank has just, in the previous minute, given three excellent reasons someone would egg his car. Perfect economy.

dialogue.speaker: Roseanne
dialogue.line: Yeah, but the only thing I remember about sex with you in the limo is that Ben was driving.

jokes.text: Hank considers who might have egged his car: 'Well... there's that fucking security guard. Then there's that fucking waitress at the commissary. Oh, no. It's the fat grip.'
jokes.setup: Hank is asked if he's had any run-ins with anyone lately
jokes.punchline: The escalating list of enemies — security guard, commissary waitress, and then the sudden horror of realizing it might be 'the fat grip' — reveals Hank has a long list of people he's wronged
jokes.explanation: The rhythm of this is excellent — the list builds and then the sudden shift to 'Oh, no. It's the fat grip.' suggests a specific and awful incident Hank has had with a production crew member. The horror in Hank's voice makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Roseanne
dialogue.line: Yeah, but the only thing I remember about sex with you in the limo is that Ben was driving.

jokes.text: Artie's assistant confuses 'Barry White' (the icon of love) with 'Betty White' when reading notes. Larry: 'These are the notes for Betty White?'
jokes.setup: Notes are brought in for Barry White's appearance
jokes.punchline: The misread — Barry/Betty — and Larry's momentary confusion creates a brief absurd image of Betty White as 'icon of love'
jokes.explanation: A functional name-confusion gag. The comedy is in the image of Betty White as 'icon of love' — mild but effective. Modest originality.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Surf's up.

jokes.text: Roseanne's message via Beverly: 'Tell that limp dick asshole if he wants to bump me he should have the balls to do it himself, or I'm going to come down there and beat his fat ass just the way he likes it.'
jokes.setup: Roseanne has called about the bump; Beverly relays the message verbatim to Larry
jokes.punchline: The full message — escalating through 'limp dick,' 'bump me,' 'balls,' to 'beat his fat ass just the way he likes it' — is a cascade of double entendres and aggressive intimacy
jokes.explanation: Beverly reading this message verbatim, with its sexual innuendo and power-play aggression, is a showcase moment. The message is perfectly constructed — 'just the way he likes it' reveals intimate knowledge while threatening violence. Beverly's professionalism in relaying it makes it funnier. High character integration for Roseanne-as-force-of-nature.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Damn it! Why couldn't she have done that on tonight's show? We would have had worldwide publicity.

jokes.text: 'Tell that limp dick asshole if he wants to bump me he should have the balls to do it himself, or I'm going to come down there and beat his fat ass just the way he likes it.'
jokes.setup: Beverly relays Roseanne's message; Larry asks for her exact words
jokes.punchline: The exact words are extraordinary — Roseanne's message is a cascade of aggressive insults culminating in the implication that Larry likes being beaten, which Beverly delivers to his face with professional neutrality
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional character comedy on multiple levels: Roseanne's voice through Beverly's neutral delivery, the specificity of 'limp dick asshole,' and the kicker 'beat his fat ass just the way he likes it' — which simultaneously insults him and implies a kink — with Beverly's professional matter-of-factness making it funnier. 'I just said that I liked it' from Larry is the perfect button. Character integration is superb: only Roseanne's character would send this message.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Dr. Reisman wanted me to run away like some little girl.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I just said that I liked it. What line is she on?' As lines 2, 3, and 4 all light up with Roseanne.
jokes.setup: Roseanne's message ends with the sadomasochistic implication; Larry processes this
jokes.punchline: Larry's only response to the implication that he enjoys being beaten is 'I just said that I liked it' — confirming it — before pivoting immediately to logistics
jokes.explanation: The speed at which Larry moves from implicitly confirming a sexual preference to 'What line is she on?' is perfect Larry behavior — his emotional life is always subordinated to logistics. Well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Bump ivanka.

jokes.text: Multiple phone lines light up — lines 2, 3, and 4 — all Roseanne. Larry: 'It's these multiple personalities, OK?' Artie: 'Perhaps you could arrange a conference call between you, Dr. Reisman, and the 12 Roseannes.'
jokes.setup: Roseanne has somehow occupied multiple phone lines simultaneously
jokes.punchline: Artie's suggestion of a conference call 'between you, Dr. Reisman, and the 12 Roseannes' — riffing on the real Roseanne's public persona around multiple personalities/childhood trauma
jokes.explanation: The '12 Roseannes' joke references Roseanne Barr's real-life claim of multiple personalities — it's insider comedy that rewards the audience for knowing. Well-constructed absurdist moment. High originality for the celebrity-specific reference.

jokes.text: Phil confronted with egg cartons, dried egg on shoe, yolk on fingers. Phil: 'Maybe it was a drug deal gone bad that led to this horrible egging. But I have to assure you, Hank, that I am 100% not guilty.'
jokes.setup: Hank has discovered Phil is covered in egg evidence
jokes.punchline: 'I am 100% not guilty' — Phil's OJ-trial language applied to the egging, mirroring the exact phrasing of OJ's public statements while caught red-handed (or yolk-handed)
jokes.explanation: Structurally elegant callback — Phil's denial using OJ trial language ('100% not guilty') while covered in obvious egg evidence mirrors OJ's own situation. The layers work: Phil is doing to Hank what Hank accused OJ's critics of doing. High earned comedy and strong callback structure.

jokes.text: You little prick. You little prick! What? You did it! You egged my car! / What are you talking about? / What am I talking... my Bentley is covered with eggs!
jokes.setup: Hank confronts Phil about the egging; Phil feigns innocence
jokes.punchline: Hank's operatic outrage — 'MY BENTLEY' — elevating a petty egg attack to a crime against luxury property
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of the egging subplot. Hank's specific hurt about the Bentley is character-appropriate vanity. The confrontation scene is well-played cringe comedy.

jokes.text: Phil comes clean to Hank: 'Fuck you, Hank. Of course I did it.' — immediately after an OJ-style not-guilty declaration
jokes.setup: Phil has maintained elaborate innocence using OJ language
jokes.punchline: The immediate snap to 'Of course I did it' demolishes the elaborate OJ parody he just performed — the joke is the speed of the confession
jokes.explanation: The whiplash from OJ-trial rhetoric to instant confession is the punchline — maximum economy. Phil's 'Fuck you, Hank. Of course I did it.' is the anti-OJ verdict. One of the episode's best moments for structural satisfaction.

jokes.text: There you are. Is that Chevy? / Yeah, you told him to stop by before the show. / Yeah, yesterday I did.
jokes.setup: Larry finds Chevy Chase hanging around backstage
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'yeah, yesterday I did' — the implication that invitations issued during psychiatric distress have a short shelf life, and Chevy has been waiting for hours
jokes.explanation: A mild callback that works as a reminder of Larry's unreliable social commitments. Not a standout but contextually appropriate.

jokes.text: Roseanne: 'I can't wear this dress! I'm pregnant, you dipshit!' Followed immediately by her screaming about the sauna-like temperature in her dressing room.
jokes.setup: Larry approaches Roseanne's dressing room nervously
jokes.punchline: Roseanne's entrance into the episode is a blast of aggression and pregnancy rage — the announcement of pregnancy via insult ('you dipshit') immediately followed by thermostat fury
jokes.explanation: Roseanne Barr playing a version of herself as force-of-nature — the pregnancy reveal via insult is perfect casting and character integration. The dressing room temperature immediately following establishes her as a human weather system.

jokes.text: Who shut that door?! / It's like a goddamn sauna in here! / Open it. Open it. Open it.
jokes.setup: Someone closes Roseanne's dressing room door after she yells about the dress
jokes.punchline: Roseanne's immediate escalation to temperature complaints — the door closes for 3 seconds and it becomes 'a goddamn sauna'
jokes.explanation: Good Roseanne character comedy — her combustibility perfectly rendered through a temperature complaint. The triple 'Open it. Open it. Open it.' is a nice rhythmic button. Character-specific but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Artie to Larry before the show: 'I smell sulfur.' — repeating his earlier line when Larry seemed to relent about Roseanne
jokes.setup: Artie tells Larry this is where he should face Roseanne — on his show, where he's in command
jokes.punchline: 'I smell sulfur' — calling back his earlier use of the phrase, now used triumphantly rather than appeasingly, signaling that the real show-confrontation is imminent
jokes.explanation: Callbacks earn their score when they add resonance, and 'I smell sulfur' doing double duty — first as sardonic commentary on drama, now as battle cry — works well. Artie's anticipatory relish is the character note.

jokes.text: On air: Roseanne and Larry greet awkwardly. Roseanne: 'That was weird.' Larry: 'What was weird?' Roseanne: 'Just then, when you didn't know whether to kiss me or not.'
jokes.setup: Larry has introduced Roseanne on air; they have a visibly awkward physical greeting
jokes.punchline: Roseanne calls out the awkwardness immediately and publicly — breaking the talk-show courtesy convention with a direct announcement of Larry's discomfort
jokes.explanation: The on-air revelation of off-air discomfort is the engine of the final act. Roseanne's ability to make private pain public is her superpower and the show's subject. Well-executed cringe with high character integration.

jokes.text: Roseanne announces the baby isn't Larry's: 'I had the ultrasound, and it couldn't be yours, because it had a penis and a brain.'
jokes.setup: Larry tries to clarify that the baby isn't his; Roseanne confirms
jokes.punchline: 'It had a penis and a brain' — the insult is that Larry lacks one or both; the specificity of the ultrasound evidence makes it funnier
jokes.explanation: The episode's single best joke. The structure is elegant — the ultrasound as forensic proof, with the evidence being a penis and brain (implying Larry has neither, or possibly just the latter). Delivered live on fictional air to a studio audience. Maximum economy — two pieces of evidence do dual comic work. High character integration — this is Roseanne at full power, Larry at full deflation. One of the episode's most quotable and memorable lines.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I believe I have one of those.' — responding to the penis and brain claim
jokes.setup: Roseanne has just said the baby couldn't be Larry's because it had a penis and a brain
jokes.punchline: Larry's meek, singular defense — 'I believe I have one of those' — without specifying which one, delivered with characteristic Larry uncertainty
jokes.explanation: The callback response is nearly as good as the original joke. The ambiguity of 'one of those' — which one? penis? brain? — is the entire joke compressed into four words. Larry's hedged self-defense is perfect character work. Outstanding economy.

jokes.text: Roseanne: 'You never wanted to actually have kids anyway, did you, Larry? Because Larry doesn't want children. He's one of those weird people who are just much too selfish to want children.'
jokes.setup: The on-air interview has turned into a public airing of private grievances
jokes.punchline: Roseanne addresses the audience about Larry's character as though she's a therapist doing a case presentation on a reluctant patient — the intimacy is weaponized publicly
jokes.explanation: Solid cringe comedy — Roseanne characterizing Larry to his own audience while he sits there. Good use of the talk-show format as a torture device for the host.

jokes.text: You never wanted to actually have kids anyway, did you, Larry? Because, you know, Larry doesn't want children. He's one of those weird people who are just much too selfish to want children.
jokes.setup: Roseanne continues her attack, now pivoting to Larry's parental ambitions
jokes.punchline: Roseanne's on-air psychoanalysis of Larry — 'much too selfish to want children' — delivered to millions while Larry sits next to her
jokes.explanation: Good cringe comedy — Roseanne publicly analyzing Larry's psychology on his own show. The specific detail 'much too selfish' is character-appropriate. The comedy is in the social transgression of doing this on television.

jokes.text: Larry's defense against not wanting children: 'I think I would feel competitive over the breast-feeding area. I think that I would be there, nudging the child out of the way.'
jokes.setup: Larry denies he's selfish about children; begins to explain his real objection
jokes.punchline: His objection is that he would compete with his own infant for breastfeeding access — the image of Larry nudging a baby aside is both absurd and psychologically revealing
jokes.explanation: This is Larry at his most confessionally bizarre — he's not refuting the selfish charge but illustrating it with a grotesque specific scenario. 'Nudging the child out of the way' is a perfectly vivid image. High character integration — this is Shandling's Larry at full neurotic stretch.

jokes.text: Larry extends the breast-feeding monologue: romantic music, a glass of wine for the breast-feeding 'as opposed to the child, who hasn't learned that technique yet.' The child 'takes it for granted... Do not take this for granted. It will be 18 years before you see another one.'
jokes.setup: Larry is elaborating on his breast-feeding rivalry with his hypothetical child
jokes.punchline: 'It will be 18 years before you see another one' — Larry's advice to his infant child about the scarcity of breast access, delivered with the gravity of hard-won wisdom
jokes.explanation: The escalation here is superb — the premise builds from absurd (competing with baby) to philosophical (the scarcity argument) to paternal advice ('18 years before you see another one'). This is Shandling-caliber stand-up material embedded in a sitcom scene. The wisdom-to-infant framing is the joke's perfect capstone.

jokes.text: Roseanne: 'I think that you were mad at me because basically I dumped you.' Larry: 'No, I dumped you, I believe.' Roseanne: 'No, I believe that I dumped you, because your idea of fun is sitting home every single night watching your own show.'
jokes.setup: The breakup's cause is being adjudicated live on air
jokes.punchline: Roseanne's evidence for dumping Larry: he watched his own show every night — the ultimate talk-show-host vanity/insecurity portrait
jokes.explanation: Watching your own show every night is the perfect comedic characterization of Larry's pathology — competitive, insecure, self-obsessed. This is also a sharp meta-comment on showbiz narcissism. High character integration and earned comedy.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Wait a minute. We watched your show.' Roseanne: 'Yeah, but my show's funny.'
jokes.setup: Larry defends himself by pointing out they watched Roseanne's show too
jokes.punchline: 'Yeah, but my show's funny.' — Roseanne's flat dismissal of the Larry Sanders Show's humor, delivered with absolute confidence
jokes.explanation: Four words. This might be the most economical joke in the episode and one of its best. 'Yeah, but my show's funny' is devastating in its simplicity — it's a direct evaluation of the meta-show itself delivered by Roseanne Barr, a celebrity playing herself, on the show it's dismissing. Perfect character integration, extraordinary economy. The confidence of the delivery (no explanation, no qualifications) is what makes it land as hard as it does.

jokes.text: Roseanne: 'You're just pissed because you caught me and my wonderful husband Ben doing it.' Larry: 'As I recall, we had sex a couple of times in the limo while Ben was driving.'
jokes.setup: Roseanne accuses Larry of being upset because he caught her with Ben
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'correction' — that they had sex while Ben drove the limo — reframes the geometry of the betrayal: it wasn't catching them, it was a three-person arrangement with Ben unwitting
jokes.explanation: The callback to the earlier limo story pays off perfectly — the story has evolved. Earlier it was humiliation (Roseanne making out with the driver); now it's revealed as a complex arrangement. The casual 'a couple of times' and 'while Ben was driving' makes the logistics darkly hilarious.

jokes.text: As I... as I recall, uh, we had, uh, sex a couple of times, uh, in the limo while Ben was driving.
jokes.setup: Roseanne brings up catching her with Ben; Larry counters with his version of events
jokes.punchline: Larry confessing to sex in a limo while the future husband was driving — an act of incredible social tone-deafness on-air — delivered with Larry's characteristic stumbling dignity
jokes.explanation: Larry's counter-revelation — that he and Roseanne had sex while Ben drove — is a great escalation. It makes Larry's complaint about the limo making-out scene retroactively more complicated and reveals his moral logic is inconsistent. The character specificity is high: Larry's oblivious revelation of damaging information about himself is a signature move.

jokes.text: Roseanne: 'Yeah, but the only thing I remember about sex with you in the limo is that Ben was driving.'
jokes.setup: Larry has just revealed they had sex in the limo with Ben driving
jokes.punchline: Roseanne confirms it — and the only memorable thing about sex with Larry is who was driving the car. Ben's presence outshone Larry entirely.
jokes.explanation: The episode's comedic peak alongside joke #55. The entire limo story — set up 20 minutes earlier, revised at 22:43, and now delivered as the ultimate deflation — pays off with devastating economy. 'The only thing I remember about sex with you is that Ben was driving' is a complete roast of Larry's sexual presence, his relationship history, and the entire arc of the episode. Perfect structure, character integration, economy, and originality in the application. This is what 9+ looks like.

jokes.text: After the interview, Artie: 'You're the funniest woman we've had on the show since Janet Reno.'
jokes.setup: The interview has concluded; Artie congratulates Roseanne
jokes.punchline: 'Since Janet Reno' — the compliment's comparator is a notoriously un-funny government official, which retroactively damns the show's female guest history
jokes.explanation: A clean, well-constructed compliment-as-insult. 'Since Janet Reno' implies the bar for funniest female guest was previously an Attorney General known for her severity. Artie delivers it as sincere praise, which is the joke.

jokes.text: Roseanne: 'I cannot believe that you tried to bump me.' Larry: 'Yeah, well, you know, I was hurt, and I tried to hurt you back, I guess.'
jokes.setup: Post-show, Larry and Roseanne have a moment of genuine resolution
jokes.punchline: Larry's admission — 'I tried to hurt you back, I guess' — delivered with his characteristic hedging 'I guess' is equal parts honest and pathetically understated given what the show just put them both through
jokes.explanation: More emotional resolution than punchline, but 'I guess' as Larry's qualifier on his own emotional honesty is a character touch. Functional rather than exceptional.

jokes.text: Roseanne's water breaks. Artie: 'Surf's up.'
jokes.setup: Roseanne's water breaks during the post-show conversation
jokes.punchline: 'Surf's up.' — Artie's response to amniotic fluid on the floor is two words of supreme deadpan
jokes.explanation: Two words. Absolute economy — 'Surf's up' is the funniest possible response to broken water, and Rip Torn's Artie is the only character on this show who would say it. No panic, no concern, no sentimentality — just the ocean metaphor applied with complete sangfroid. This is a hall-of-fame-tier button line. Exceptionally high economy score (10/10 — it cannot be shorter or better).

jokes.text: Artie backstage after Roseanne's water breaks: 'Why couldn't she have done that on tonight's show? We would have had worldwide publicity.'
jokes.setup: Roseanne's water has broken and she's being attended to
jokes.punchline: Artie's only regret is that it didn't happen on air — his producer instincts override all human concern
jokes.explanation: Pure Artie — the world ends and he thinks about the ratings. 'Worldwide publicity' from Roseanne's water breaking on air is grotesquely funny because it's completely true and completely monstrous. This is the show's central satirical theme (showbiz indifference to human experience) compressed into two sentences.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Dr. Reisman wanted me to run away like some little girl.' — post-show triumphalism
jokes.setup: Larry is feeling good about having faced Roseanne; credits Artie
jokes.punchline: Larry's dismissal of the therapist's advice ('run away like some little girl') is both triumphant and oblivious — the therapy session was what actually gave him perspective, filtered through Artie's blunter wisdom
jokes.explanation: A satisfying ironic callback — Larry credits Artie while dismissing the therapist, not realizing the therapy was instrumental. The 'little girl' phrasing is a mild joke with moderate impact.

jokes.text: Episode ends: Artie announces tomorrow's show has 'Ivanka, Blues Traveler, and Kato Kaelin.' Larry: 'No, no, no. Bump Ivanka.'
jokes.setup: Having just faced his ex on air, Larry is now addressed about tomorrow's lineup
jokes.punchline: 'Bump Ivanka' — after spending the entire episode trying not to face Roseanne, Larry now casually bumps the supermodel he had dinner with, without explanation
jokes.explanation: The episode's structural closing joke — the entire Roseanne drama has been about bumping; now Larry casually bumps the woman who was supposed to make him forget Roseanne. It's a callback to the show's entire thematics (Larry's inability to commit, his casual cruelty, the revolving door of talent) delivered in two words. Strong economy and structural payoff.

tmdb_overview: Larry is apprehensive over a guest appearance by former girl friend Roseanne and decides to see a psychiatrist. The office follows the O.J. trial.
